results.text:
I found 30 of the 300 CpGs differentially methylated between tumor and normal at BH-adjusted p < 0.05. Only 16 of those also have |Δβ| > 0.1, and the data have a problem that limits how far you can trust the p-values.

**Method.** The design is paired, with 4 patients each contributing one tumor and one normal sample. I converted the betas to logit M-values and ran a paired t-test per CpG, which is the same as a patient-adjusted tissue effect. I report the effect as Δβ (tumor minus normal) and applied Benjamini–Hochberg correction across all 300 CpGs. There were no missing values and the betas span 0.01–0.99. The design, scale and filter are stated at the top of `scripts/dmp.py`.

**Results** (`output/tumor_vs_normal_results.csv`, 300 rows sorted by p-value):
- The strongest hits are hypomethylated in tumor, for example cg10000111 (Δβ −0.34, adjusted p = 2e-8), cg10000296 (−0.32) and cg10000629 (−0.40).
- The table has the Δβ, p-value and adjusted p-value for every CpG, plus the mean beta in tumor and normal and the logit difference.

**Caveats:**
- **Tiny effects pass the FDR cut.** Several of the 30 hits, such as cg10006623 and cg10009287, have |Δβ| ≈ 0.001 with adjusted p < 1e-5. This happens because their paired differences are almost identical across patients, so the variance is close to zero. I would not call these biologically meaningful, so use an effect-size cut-off as well (for example |Δβ| > 0.1, which leaves 16 CpGs).
- **The samples look duplicated.** T1 and T3 correlate at 1.000 across CpGs, as do T2 and T4, N1 and N3, and N2 and N4. The first rows also show T3 equal to T1 and T4 equal to T2. This suggests the four patients are really two distinct profiles, or that the data were simulated or duplicated upstream. If so, the replicates are not independent, and the p-values are overstated. Please check the sample provenance before relying on the p-values.
- **Power and scale.** With n = 4 pairs and 300 CpGs, power is low. The 300 CpGs are an already filtered set, not a whole array. I did no cell-composition adjustment, and tumor purity could contribute to the differences.

Files are in `/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1`:
- `scripts/dmp.py`
- `output/tumor_vs_normal_results.csv`

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, json
from scipy.stats import hypergeom
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
IN = "/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1/output/"
GMT = "/mnt/refs/go/c5.go.bp.v2024.1.Hs.symbols.gmt"
MIN_SET, MAX_SET, JAC = 5, 500, 0.5

dmp = pd.read_csv(IN + "dmp_results.csv")
bg = set(pd.read_csv(IN + "tested_cpgs_per_gene.csv").gene)
hits = set(dmp.gene.dropna()) & bg
print("hit genes", len(set(dmp.gene)), "in background", len(hits), "bg", len(bg))

sets = {}
for l in open(GMT):
    p = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
    sets[p[0]] = set(p[2:])
mapped_bg = set().union(*sets.values()) & bg
rows = []
N = len(mapped_bg); hits_m = hits & mapped_bg; n = len(hits_m)
for t, g in sets.items():
    gb = g & mapped_bg
    if not (MIN_SET <= len(gb) <= MAX_SET): continue
    o = hits_m & gb
    if len(o) < 2: continue
    p = hypergeom.sf(len(o) - 1, N, len(gb), n)
    rows.append(dict(term=t, collection="MSigDB C5 GO:BP", test="hypergeometric ORA", set_size=len(gb),
                     overlap=len(o), pvalue=p, genes=";".join(sorted(o))))
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df["adjusted_pvalue"] = multipletests(df.pvalue, method="fdr_bh")[1]
df = df.sort_values("pvalue").reset_index(drop=True)
# group significant terms by shared genes (greedy, Jaccard)
df["group"] = ""
sig = df[df.adjusted_pvalue < 0.05]
reps = []
for i, r in sig.iterrows():
    gs = set(r.genes.split(";"))
    for k, (ri, rg) in enumerate(reps):
        if len(gs & rg) / len(gs | rg) >= JAC:
            df.loc[i, "group"] = f"G{k+1}"; break
    else:
        reps.append((i, gs)); df.loc[i, "group"] = f"G{len(reps)}"
df = df[["term","collection","test","set_size","overlap","pvalue","adjusted_pvalue","genes","group"]]
df.to_csv("output/enrichment_results.csv", index=False)
json.dump(dict(collection="MSigDB C5 GO:BP (gene symbols)", release="2024.1.Hs", test="one-sided hypergeometric ORA, BH FDR; gene-level (unique genes of DMPs FDR<0.05)",
               background_size=N, tested_genes=len(bg), hit_genes=len(hits), hit_genes_mapped=n,
               mapped_fraction_background=N/len(bg), mapped_fraction_hits=n/len(hits),
               terms_tested=len(df), terms_fdr05=int((df.adjusted_pvalue<0.05).sum()),
               set_size_filter=[MIN_SET, MAX_SET], grouping=f"greedy Jaccard>={JAC} on overlap genes"),
          open("output/enrichment_summary.json", "w"), indent=1)
print(df.head(15).to_string()); print((df.adjusted_pvalue<0.05).sum(), len(df))

# GO:BP enrichment of differentially methylated genes

Test: one-sided hypergeometric over-representation, BH FDR. Source: MSigDB C5 GO:BP 2024.1.Hs (symbols).
Hits: 53 unique genes carrying DMPs (FDR<0.05, 108 sites). Background: the 220 genes tested in T1S1, of which 207 map to the collection (94%). 51 of 53 hits map (96%).
Script: `scripts/go_ora.py`. Results: `output/enrichment_results.csv`, `output/enrichment_summary.json`.

## Result (2 of 12 terms at adjusted p < 0.05)
| term | overlap / set size | adjusted p |
|---|---|---|
| GOBP_RESPONSE_TO_HYPOXIA | 18 / 30 | 8.8e-5 |
| GOBP_SYNAPTIC_SIGNALING | 19 / 36 | 3.1e-4 |

The other 10 terms have adjusted p ≥ 0.85.
The two significant terms share few genes, so they stay in separate groups (G1, G2).

## Caveats
- The GMT in the reference store yields only 12 testable terms (set sizes 20–36 within the background). That is not the full GO:BP collection, which has thousands of terms. The multiple-testing burden is small and the results are limited to these 12 terms. Treat the file as a curated or truncated subset.
- The background is a 220-gene targeted set, not the genome. Enrichment is relative to that set.
- Genes with more CpGs tested have more chances to carry a DMP (e.g. ACTB, 112 CpGs). This test is gene-level and does not correct for that. Some enrichment may reflect CpG count rather than biology. A CpG-count-aware test (e.g. a logistic or weighted model) was not run.
- Hits were not split by hyper- or hypomethylation direction.
- The enrichment is an association with curated gene sets. It does not show that these processes are altered in the tumors. Methylation effects on gene function were not tested.

results.text:
Two GO biological processes are enriched among the genes with differentially methylated sites, at adjusted p < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg).

| GO term | Overlap / set size | Adjusted p |
|---|---|---|
| Response to hypoxia | 18 / 30 | 8.8e-5 |
| Synaptic signaling | 19 / 36 | 3.1e-4 |

The two terms share few genes, so I kept them as separate groups. The other 10 tested terms have adjusted p ≥ 0.85.

**Method:** I ran a one-sided hypergeometric over-representation test on the 53 unique genes carrying the 108 significant sites from the differential methylation step. The background was the 220 genes tested in that step. Of the 220 background genes, 207 (94%) map to the GO collection, and 51 of the 53 hits (96%) map. The collection is MSigDB C5 GO biological process, release 2024.1.Hs.

**Caveats:**
- **Only 12 terms were testable.** Within this background, only 12 GO terms (set sizes 20–36) were testable. The GO file in the reference store looks like a curated or truncated subset, not the full collection. That makes the multiple-testing burden small and limits what the result can say.
- **The background is small.** The 220 genes are a targeted set rather than the whole genome, so enrichment is relative to that set.
- **CpG count is not corrected.** Genes with more CpGs tested have more chances to carry a hit (ACTB, for example, has 112 tested). Part of the enrichment could reflect CpG count rather than biology. I did not run a test that corrects for this.
- **Direction is not split.** I did not separate hypermethylated from hypomethylated sites.
- **This is an association only.** The enrichment is consistent with these processes being involved, but it does not show that they are altered in the tumors.

Files are in `/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S2`:
- `output/enrichment_results.csv`
- `output/enrichment_summary.json`

- `scripts/go_ora.py`

IN = "/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1/output/"
MIN_SET, MAX_SET, JACCARD = 3, 500, 0.5

all_gmt = set().union(*sets.values())

    p = hypergeom.sf(len(ov) - 1, N, len(g), n)

                     set_size=len(g), overlap=len(ov), pvalue=p, genes=";".join(sorted(ov))))

# group significant-ish terms (adj<0.25) by shared hit genes, greedy by p
res["group"] = ""
cand = res[res.adjusted_pvalue < 0.25]
reps = []
for i, r in cand.iterrows():
    gs = set(r.genes.split(";"))

    else:
        reps.append((i, gs)); res.at[i, "group"] = f"G{len(reps)}"

res.to_csv("output/enrichment_results.csv", index=False)
json.dump(dict(collection="MSigDB C5 GO:BP (symbols)", release="2024.1.Hs", test="one-sided hypergeometric ORA, BH FDR",
               background_size=N, n_hits=n, n_terms_tested=len(res), min_set=MIN_SET, max_set=MAX_SET,
               mapped_fraction=round(mapped, 3), hits_mapped_fraction=round(hits_mapped, 3),
               n_sig_fdr05=int((res.adjusted_pvalue < .05).sum())),

Two GO biological process terms are enriched among the 53 genes with differentially methylated sites. Both pass FDR < 0.05, and neither holds up as a clear-cut biological finding. The full table is in `output/enrichment_results.csv`.

| Term | Set size in background | Hit genes in set | p | Adjusted p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GOBP_RESPONSE_TO_HYPOXIA | 30 | 18 | 6e-6 | 6.6e-5 |
| GOBP_SYNAPTIC_SIGNALING | 36 | 19 | 3.9e-5 | 2.4e-4 |

The other 10 terms have adjusted p of 0.83 or higher (the best one, cell cycle process, has p = 0.34).

**Method**
- **Test:** one-sided hypergeometric over-representation test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
- **Gene sets:** MSigDB C5 GO:BP release 2024.1.Hs, using gene symbols.
- **Hits:** the 53 unique genes carrying DSS sites at FDR < 0.05 from T1S1. All 53 are in the background.
- **Background:** the 220 genes with tested CpGs in T1S1, not the whole genome.
- **Mapping:** 94% of the background and 96% of the hits map to the GO collection.
- **Set size filter:** sets of 3 to 500 genes after restriction to the background. Only 12 terms overlapped any hit, so the correction covers just 12 tests.

**Caveats**
- **Direction:** I did not split the hits into hyper- and hypomethylated genes. Enrichment shows which processes the genes belong to, not whether methylation goes up or down.
- **Bias:** this is a targeted gene panel, so the result only says these processes are over-represented relative to the panel. The tested CpG count per gene varies a lot (ACTB has 112), and genes with more CpGs have more chances to be hits. I did not correct for this, which could inflate enrichment for terms rich in heavily covered genes.
- **Gene sets:** the sets in this file are small (20 to 36 genes within the background). Several memberships look unusual, for example ACTB, CCND1 and SMAD4 under "synaptic signaling". Treat that label with caution. The hypoxia and synaptic-signaling terms share no hit genes, so they are separate signals.
- **Interpretation:** the enrichment is consistent with hypoxia-related genes being differentially methylated. It does not show a mechanism.

**Files**
- `output/enrichment_results.csv`
- `output/enrichment_summary.json`
- `scripts/go_ora.py`

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, json
from scipy.stats import fisher_exact
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
GMT = "/mnt/refs/go/c5.go.bp.v2024.1.Hs.symbols.gmt"
D = "/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1/output/"
MIN, MAX, JACC = 3, 500, 0.5
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
dmp = pd.read_csv(D + "dmp_results.csv")
bg = pd.read_csv(D + "tested_cpgs_per_gene.csv")
hits = set(dmp.gene.unique()); universe = set(bg.gene)
assert hits <= universe
sets = {}
for l in open(GMT):
    p = l.rstrip("\n").split("\t"); sets[p[0]] = set(p[2:]) & universe
mapped = len(universe & set().union(*sets.values())) / len(universe)
rows = []
for t, g in sets.items():
    if not MIN <= len(g) <= MAX: continue
    k = len(g & hits)
    if k < 2: continue
    a = k; b = len(hits) - k; c = len(g) - k; d = len(universe) - len(hits) - c
    _, p = fisher_exact([[a, b], [c, d]], alternative="greater")
    rows.append((t, len(g), k, p, ";".join(sorted(g & hits))))
r = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["term", "set_size", "overlap", "pvalue", "genes"])
r["adjusted_pvalue"] = multipletests(r.pvalue, method="fdr_bh")[1]
r["collection"] = "MSigDB C5 GO:BP 2024.1"; r["test"] = "Fisher ORA (one-sided), background=tested genes"
# CpG-count-biased check: sample gene sets of same size with prob ~ n_cpgs
w = bg.set_index("gene").n_cpgs_tested; w = (w / w.sum())
ug = np.array(sorted(universe)); pw = w.loc[ug].values
perm = [set(ug[rng.choice(len(ug), len(hits), replace=False, p=pw)]) for _ in range(2000)]
r["bias_adjusted_perm_p"] = [(1 + sum(len(s & set(gs.split(";"))) >= ov for s in perm) * 0 + 0) for gs, ov in zip(r.genes, r.overlap)]
r["bias_adjusted_perm_p"] = [(1 + sum(len(s & set(sets[t])) >= ov for s in perm)) / (len(perm) + 1) for t, ov in zip(r.term, r.overlap)]
# group terms by shared hit genes (greedy, Jaccard)
r = r.sort_values("pvalue").reset_index(drop=True)
grp = []; reps = []
for i, gs in enumerate(r.genes):
    s = set(gs.split(";"))
    for j, rs in reps:
        if len(s & rs) / len(s | rs) >= JACC: grp.append(j); break
    else: reps.append((i, s)); grp.append(i)
r["group"] = ["G%d:%s" % (reps_i, r.term[reps_i]) for reps_i in grp]
r = r[["term","collection","test","set_size","overlap","pvalue","adjusted_pvalue","bias_adjusted_perm_p","genes","group"]]
r.to_csv("output/enrichment_results.csv", index=False)
json.dump(dict(collection="MSigDB C5 GO:BP", release="2024.1.Hs", test="one-sided Fisher ORA, BH; sets %d-%d genes in universe, overlap>=2" % (MIN, MAX),
    background_size=len(universe), n_hit_genes=len(hits), n_terms_tested=len(r), mapped_fraction=mapped), open("output/enrichment_summary.json", "w"), indent=1)
print(mapped, len(r), (r.adjusted_pvalue < .05).sum())
print(r[r.adjusted_pvalue < .1].head(25)[["term","set_size","overlap","adjusted_pvalue","bias_adjusted_perm_p","group"]].to_string())

results.text:
Yes, the hit genes share one process, response to hypoxia. A second term, synaptic signaling, is significant on the standard test but probably reflects how many CpGs each gene had.

I ran an over-representation test (one-sided Fisher). The 53 genes with a significant site (FDR < 0.05) were tested against a background of the 220 genes tested in T1S1. The gene sets were GO biological process terms from MSigDB C5, release 2024.1. I kept sets with 3–500 genes in the background and at least 2 hits, which left 12 terms. P-values are Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted across those 12.

| Process | Genes in set (of 220) | Hits | Adjusted p | Adjusted p, CpG-count-matched permutation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Response to hypoxia | 30 | 18 | 6.6e-5 | 0.0005 |
| Synaptic signaling | 36 | 19 | 2.4e-4 | 0.94 |

No other term reached FDR < 0.05 (all 12 are in `output/enrichment_results.csv`).

- **Hypoxia:** The signal holds up when I sample random gene sets weighted by the number of CpGs tested per gene. The gene list is in the `genes` column of `output/enrichment_results.csv`. This is consistent with a hypoxia-related response, but it is an association with a curated gene set, not evidence of mechanism.
- **Synaptic signaling:** Treat this as not supported. It does not survive the CpG-count-matched permutation, so it probably reflects that genes with more CpGs tested are more likely to be called. The permutation p-values are my own check and are not adjusted for multiple testing.
- **Term grouping:** I grouped terms that share their hit genes (Jaccard ≥ 0.5). Neither significant term merged with another, so these are two separate signals.

Limits:
- The background is only 220 genes, and 94% of them map to GO:BP. This is a small, probably pre-selected panel, so the power is low and the results are specific to this panel, not the genome.
- The hit list contains several sites per gene, such as ANGPTL4 with at least three. I tested at the gene level, so the test counts each gene once.
- The test does not use the direction of methylation change.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, subprocess, os
from cyvcf2 import VCF
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib; matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

VCFP = "/analysis-001/data/inputs/f-geno/cohort.vcf.gz"
PHEN = "/analysis-001/data/inputs/f-geno/pheno.txt"
NPC, MAF_MIN, HWE_MIN, MISS_MAX = 10, 0.01, 1e-6, 0.02
GW, SUG = 5e-8, 1e-5
for d in ("output", "figures", "logs"): os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)

ph = pd.read_csv(PHEN, sep="\t")
v = VCF(VCFP); samples = list(v.samples)
assert set(ph.IID) == set(samples)
y = ph.set_index("IID").loc[samples, "PHENO1"].values.astype(float)
print("pheno NaN:", np.isnan(y).sum())

meta, G = [], []
for r in v:
    gt = np.array(r.genotypes)[:, :2]
    miss = (gt < 0).any(1)
    d = np.where(miss, np.nan, gt.sum(1).astype(float))
    meta.append((r.ID, r.CHROM, r.POS, r.REF, r.ALT[0])); G.append(d)
G = np.array(G)  # variants x samples
m = pd.DataFrame(meta, columns=["variant_id", "chromosome", "position", "ref", "alt"])
m["chromosome"] = m.chromosome.str.replace("chr", "")
n_called = (~np.isnan(G)).sum(1)
m["missingness"] = 1 - n_called / G.shape[1]
m["effect_allele_frequency"] = np.nanmean(G, 1) / 2
p = m.effect_allele_frequency.values
maf = np.minimum(p, 1 - p)
n0 = (G == 0).sum(1); n1 = (G == 1).sum(1); n2 = (G == 2).sum(1)
nn = n0 + n1 + n2
e0, e1, e2 = nn*(1-p)**2, nn*2*p*(1-p), nn*p**2
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    chi = sum(np.where(e > 0, (o-e)**2/e, 0) for o, e in ((n0, e0), (n1, e1), (n2, e2)))
m["hwe_p"] = stats.chi2.sf(chi, 1)
m["maf"] = maf
filt = np.where(m.missingness > MISS_MAX, "HighMissing",
        np.where(maf < MAF_MIN, "LowMAF", np.where(m.hwe_p < HWE_MIN, "HWE", "PASS")))
m["FILTER"] = filt
print(pd.Series(filt).value_counts())
keep = filt == "PASS"

# filtered VCF with populated FILTER (header + records rewritten)
fl = m.set_index(["chromosome", "position"])["FILTER"].to_dict()
with open("logs/filter_map.tsv", "w") as f:
    for (c, pos), s in fl.items(): f.write(f"chr{c}\t{pos}\t{s}\n")
hdr = ('##FILTER=<ID=HighMissing,Description="Missingness > 0.02">\n'
       '##FILTER=<ID=LowMAF,Description="MAF < 0.01">\n'
       '##FILTER=<ID=HWE,Description="HWE p < 1e-6">\n')
open("logs/hdr.txt", "w").write(hdr)
subprocess.run(f"""bcftools view {VCFP} | python3 -c "
import sys
fm={{(l.split()[0],l.split()[1]):l.split()[2] for l in open('logs/filter_map.tsv')}}
h=open('logs/hdr.txt').read()
for l in sys.stdin:
    if l.startswith('##contig') or l.startswith('##'):
        sys.stdout.write(l); continue
    if l.startswith('#CHROM'): sys.stdout.write(h); sys.stdout.write(l); continue
    t=l.split('\\t'); t[6]=fm[(t[0],t[1])]; sys.stdout.write('\\t'.join(t))
" | bgzip -c > output/filtered.vcf.gz && tabix -f -p vcf output/filtered.vcf.gz""", shell=True, check=True)

# PCA + relatedness on QC-passing variants (mean-imputed, standardized)
Gk = G[keep].copy(); pk = np.nanmean(Gk, 1, keepdims=True)
Gk = np.where(np.isnan(Gk), pk, Gk)
Z = (Gk - pk) / np.sqrt(2 * (pk/2) * (1 - pk/2))
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Z.T / np.sqrt(Z.shape[0]), full_matrices=False)
PCs = U[:, :NPC] * S[:NPC]
print("PC var explained:", np.round(S[:NPC]**2 / (S**2).sum(), 4))
K = Z.T @ Z / Z.shape[0]
off = K[np.triu_indices_from(K, 1)]
print("GRM off-diag max, #pairs >0.177:", off.max(), (off > 0.177).sum())
pd.DataFrame(PCs, index=samples, columns=[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(NPC)]).to_csv("output/pcs.csv")

# association: OLS y ~ dosage + PCs, vectorised
def assoc(Gm, covar):
    X0 = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), covar])
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(X0)
    yr = y - Q @ (Q.T @ y)
    out = []
    for g in Gm:
        ok = ~np.isnan(g)
        gg = g[ok]; Qo = Q[ok]; yo = y[ok]
        # re-residualise on the observed subset
        Q2, _ = np.linalg.qr(X0[ok])
        gr = gg - Q2 @ (Q2.T @ gg); yr2 = yo - Q2 @ (Q2.T @ yo)
        ss = gr @ gr
        b = (gr @ yr2) / ss
        res = yr2 - b * gr
        df = ok.sum() - X0.shape[1] - 1
        se = np.sqrt(res @ res / df / ss)
        out.append((b, se, 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(b / se), df), ok.sum()))
    return np.array(out)

def lam(pv): return np.median(stats.chi2.isf(pv, 1)) / stats.chi2.ppf(0.5, 1)

Gp = G[keep]; mk = m[keep].reset_index(drop=True)
r_pc = assoc(Gp, PCs)
r_no = assoc(Gp, np.empty((len(y), 0)))
lam_pc, lam_no = lam(r_pc[:, 2]), lam(r_no[:, 2])
print("lambda GC with PCs:", lam_pc, " without:", lam_no)

res = mk[["variant_id", "chromosome", "position", "ref", "alt"]].copy()
res["effect_allele"] = mk.alt
res["effect"] = r_pc[:, 0]; res["effect_scale"] = "mg/dL per alt allele (linear, ~PC1-10 adjusted)"
res["standard_error"] = r_pc[:, 1]; res["pvalue"] = r_pc[:, 2]
res["effect_allele_frequency"] = mk.effect_allele_frequency; res["n"] = r_pc[:, 3].astype(int)
res["pvalue_no_pc_adjustment"] = r_no[:, 2]
res = res.sort_values("pvalue")
res.to_csv("output/association_results.csv", index=False)
res[res.pvalue < SUG].to_csv("output/significant_variants.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame({"metric": ["n_variants_total", "n_variants_tested", "n_samples", "n_PCs", "lambda_GC_PC_adjusted",
              "lambda_GC_unadjusted", "genome_wide_threshold", "bonferroni_threshold", "n_genomewide", "n_suggestive"],
              "value": [len(m), len(mk), len(y), NPC, lam_pc, lam_no, GW, 0.05/len(mk),
                        (res.pvalue < GW).sum(), (res.pvalue < SUG).sum()]}).to_csv("output/summary_metrics.csv", index=False)

# QQ plot
plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5.5))
for pv, lab, c in ((r_no[:, 2], f"No PC adjustment (λ={lam_no:.3f})", "#fdae61"),
                   (r_pc[:, 2], f"{NPC} PCs adjusted (λ={lam_pc:.3f})", "#440154")):
    s = np.sort(pv); k = len(s)
    exp = -np.log10((np.arange(1, k+1) - 0.5) / k)
    ax.scatter(exp, -np.log10(s), s=8, c=c, label=lab)
mx = max(exp.max(), -np.log10(r_pc[:, 2].min()), -np.log10(r_no[:, 2].min())) * 1.05
ax.plot([0, exp.max()], [0, exp.max()], "k--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Expected -log10(p)"); ax.set_ylabel("Observed -log10(p)")
ax.set_title(f"QQ plot, LDL cholesterol (n={len(y)}, {len(mk)} variants)"); ax.legend(loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("figures/qq_plot.png", dpi=300); fig.savefig("figures/qq_plot.pdf")

results.text:
Two variants reach genome-wide significance for LDL cholesterol, and a third is suggestive. I did no annotation, so I haven't assigned these to genes.

The model was linear regression of LDL (mg/dL) on alt-allele dosage plus the top 10 genotype principal components. I used GRCh38 coordinates, 600 samples and 2,995 variants tested.

| Variant | Chr:position | Effect (mg/dL per G allele) | SE | p-value | G allele frequency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| rs100900 | 21:9975700 | +13.5 | 1.59 | 1.7e-16 | 0.43 |
| rs100100 | 13:1997300 | +12.8 | 2.02 | 5.7e-10 | 0.195 |
| rs102500 | 15:25932500 | +10.1 | 2.08 | 1.6e-6 | 0.19 |

- **Thresholds:** the first two pass genome-wide significance (5e-8). rs102500 passes the Bonferroni threshold for this panel (1.7e-5, i.e. 0.05/2,995) and my suggestive threshold (1e-5) but not 5e-8.
- **Next hit:** rs101694 (p = 3.9e-5) misses even the Bonferroni threshold.
- **Population structure:** the cohort has two ancestries, and PC1 explains 3.8% of variance while each later PC explains about 0.3%. Without PC adjustment the genomic inflation factor (λGC) is 3.72. With 10 PCs it is 0.996, so the adjusted model shows no residual inflation.
- **Why the PCs matter:** some unadjusted hits are ancestry artefacts, for example rs100331 (p = 3e-8 unadjusted, 6e-4 adjusted). rs100900 would also have been much weaker unadjusted (p = 1.9e-8).
- **Relatedness:** the largest pairwise relatedness estimate was 0.11, below the 0.177 cutoff for first-degree-or-closer relatives, so I kept all samples.
- **Variant filtering:** all 3,000 input calls were already PASS. I applied missingness above 0.02, minor allele frequency below 0.01 and Hardy-Weinberg p below 1e-6. Five variants failed Hardy-Weinberg and are marked `HWE` in the filtered VCF and left out of the tests. None failed on missingness or frequency.
- **Caveats:**
  - With only 600 samples, effect sizes of 10–13 mg/dL per allele are probably overestimated (winner's curse).
  - These are single-variant tests with no fine-mapping.
  - No LD reference was available, so I couldn't check whether the hits are independent signals.
  - The PCs and the relatedness check come from the same 2,995 variants, a small panel.

The p-values are exact least-squares results from my own code, not PLINK output. `plink2` is not installed here.

Files are in `/analysis-001/runs/run-001/T1S1`:
- `output/association_results.csv` (effect, SE and p-value for every variant)
- `figures/qq_plot.png` and `figures/qq_plot.pdf` (QQ plot, with and without PC adjustment)
- `output/significant_variants.csv` (variants with p < 1e-5)
- `output/summary_metrics.csv`
- `output/filtered.vcf.gz`
- `output/pcs.csv`
- `scripts/gwas.py`
